summary.text: Induction on five-term blocks, using the sequence recurrence and \(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\), gives \(a(5k),\ldots,a(5k+4)=(-1)^kF_{5k},\,(-1)^kF_{5k+1},\,(-1)^kF_{5k+1},\,0,\,(-1)^{k+1}F_{5k+3}\). Splitting an arbitrary index by its residue modulo \(5\) and taking absolute values then yields a Fibonacci number in every case.

full_proof.text:
Let the Fibonacci numbers be denoted by \(F_j\), with
\[
F_0=0,\qquad F_1=1,\qquad F_{j+2}=F_{j+1}+F_j.
\]
We first identify the recurrence for the sequence in the statement, and then prove a stronger formula describing its terms in blocks of five.

A Riordan array \((g(x),f(x))\) acts on an ordinary generating function \(B(x)\) by
\[
B(x)\longmapsto g(x)B(f(x)).
\]
The generating function of the negated Fibonacci numbers is
\[
B(x)=-\frac{x}{1-x-x^2}.
\]
Applying first the Chebyshev transform
\[
\left(\frac1{1+x^2},\frac{x}{1+x^2}\right)
\]
gives
\[
C(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}B\!\left(\frac{x}{1+x^2}\right)
     =-\frac{x}{x^4-x^3+x^2-x+1}.
\]
Applying next the binomial involution
\[
\left(\frac1{1-x},-\frac{x}{1-x}\right)
\]
gives
\[
A(x)=\frac1{1-x}C\!\left(-\frac{x}{1-x}\right)
=\frac{x(1-x)^2}{1-3x+4x^2-2x^3+x^4}.
\]
Write
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}a_nx^n.
\]
Multiplying by the denominator yields
\[
(1-3x+4x^2-2x^3+x^4)A(x)=x-2x^2+x^3.
\]
Comparison of the coefficients of \(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3\) gives
\[
a_0=0,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_2=1,\qquad a_3=0.
\]
For every \(n\geq4\), comparison of the coefficient of \(x^n\) gives the homogeneous recurrence
\[
a_n=3a_{n-1}-4a_{n-2}+2a_{n-3}-a_{n-4}. \tag{1}
\]
Thus this recurrence and these four initial values uniquely describe the Riordan-transform sequence.

Define
\[
\varepsilon_k=(-1)^k.
\]
In particular, \(\varepsilon_0=1\), \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=-\varepsilon_k\), and every \(\varepsilon_k\) is either \(1\) or \(-1\).

We claim the following stronger five-term block formula: for every \(k\geq0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{5k}&=\varepsilon_kF_{5k},\\
a_{5k+1}&=\varepsilon_kF_{5k+1},\\
a_{5k+2}&=\varepsilon_kF_{5k+1},\\
a_{5k+3}&=0,\\
a_{5k+4}&=-\varepsilon_kF_{5k+3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
We prove (2) by induction on \(k\).

For \(k=0\), the first four assertions say
\[
a_0=F_0=0,\quad a_1=F_1=1,\quad a_2=F_1=1,\quad a_3=0,
\]
which are the initial conditions. The recurrence at the next index gives
\[
a_4=3a_3-4a_2+2a_1-a_0=0-4+2-0=-2=-F_3.
\]
Since \(\varepsilon_0=1\) and \(F_3=2\), this is precisely the fifth assertion. Hence (2) holds for \(k=0\).

Now suppose (2) holds for a fixed \(k\). Put
\[
s=5k,\qquad p=F_s,\qquad q=F_{s+1},\qquad e=\varepsilon_k.
\]
Repeated use of the Fibonacci recurrence gives
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
F_{s+2}=p+q,&F_{s+3}=p+2q,&F_{s+4}=2p+3q,\\
F_{s+5}=3p+5q,&F_{s+6}=5p+8q,&F_{s+7}=8p+13q,\\
&&F_{s+8}=13p+21q.
\end{array} \tag{3}
\]
The induction hypothesis, expressed in this notation, is
\[
a_s=ep,\qquad a_{s+1}=eq,\qquad a_{s+2}=eq,\qquad a_{s+3}=0,
\qquad a_{s+4}=-e(p+2q). \tag{4}
\]
Here the last equality uses \(F_{s+3}=p+2q\).

We now apply recurrence (1) successively five times. First,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{s+5}
&=3a_{s+4}-4a_{s+3}+2a_{s+2}-a_{s+1}\\
&=3[-e(p+2q)]-4\cdot0+2eq-eq\\
&=-e(3p+5q)\\
&=-eF_{s+5},
\end{aligned} \tag{5}
\]
where the last step uses (3). Next,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{s+6}
&=3a_{s+5}-4a_{s+4}+2a_{s+3}-a_{s+2}\\
&=3[-e(3p+5q)]-4[-e(p+2q)]+0-eq\\
&=e(-9p-15q+4p+8q-q)\\
&=-e(5p+8q)\\
&=-eF_{s+6}. 
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
For the following term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{s+7}
&=3a_{s+6}-4a_{s+5}+2a_{s+4}-a_{s+3}\\
&=3[-e(5p+8q)]-4[-e(3p+5q)]+2[-e(p+2q)]-0\\
&=e(-15p-24q+12p+20q-2p-4q)\\
&=-e(5p+8q)\\
&=-eF_{s+6}. 
\end{aligned} \tag{7}
\]
The fourth new term vanishes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{s+8}
&=3a_{s+7}-4a_{s+6}+2a_{s+5}-a_{s+4}\\
&=3[-e(5p+8q)]-4[-e(5p+8q)]
   +2[-e(3p+5q)]-[-e(p+2q)]\\
&=e[(-15p-24q)+(20p+32q)+(-6p-10q)+(p+2q)]\\
&=0. 
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{s+9}
&=3a_{s+8}-4a_{s+7}+2a_{s+6}-a_{s+5}\\
&=0-4[-e(5p+8q)]+2[-e(5p+8q)]-[-e(3p+5q)]\\
&=e[(20p+32q)-(10p+16q)+(3p+5q)]\\
&=e(13p+21q)\\
&=eF_{s+8}. 
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]

Since \(s=5k\), we have \(s+5=5(k+1)\). Also
\[
\varepsilon_{k+1}=-\varepsilon_k=-e.
\]
Consequently equations (5)--(9) can be rewritten as
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{5(k+1)}&=\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{5(k+1)},\\
a_{5(k+1)+1}&=\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+1},\\
a_{5(k+1)+2}&=\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+1},\\
a_{5(k+1)+3}&=0,\\
a_{5(k+1)+4}&=-\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{5(k+1)+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, the last equation follows because (9) says
\(a_{s+9}=eF_{s+8}\), while
\(-\varepsilon_{k+1}=e\), and
\(s+8=5(k+1)+3\). This proves the induction step, and therefore establishes the block formula (2) for every \(k\geq0\).

It remains to deduce the conjecture. Let \(n\geq0\). By Euclidean division by five, there are unique integers \(k\geq0\) and \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\) such that
\[
n=5k+r.
\]
We split according to \(r\).

* If \(r=0\), then by (2),
  \[
  a_n=\varepsilon_kF_{5k},
  \]
  so \(|a_n|=F_{5k}\).

* If \(r=1\), then
  \[
  a_n=\varepsilon_kF_{5k+1},
  \]
  so \(|a_n|=F_{5k+1}\).

* If \(r=2\), then
  \[
  a_n=\varepsilon_kF_{5k+1},
  \]
  so again \(|a_n|=F_{5k+1}\).

* If \(r=3\), then \(a_n=0\), and therefore
  \[
  |a_n|=0=F_0.
  \]

* If \(r=4\), then
  \[
  a_n=-\varepsilon_kF_{5k+3},
  \]
  so \(|a_n|=F_{5k+3}\).

In each nonzero case the sign is irrelevant because \(\varepsilon_k\in\{1,-1\}\), and Fibonacci numbers are nonnegative. Thus, for every \(n\geq0\), there exists an index \(m\geq0\) such that
\[
|a_n|=F_m.
\]
Explicitly, according as \(n\equiv0,1,2,3,4\pmod5\), one may take
\[
m=5k,\quad 5k+1,\quad 5k+1,\quad 0,\quad 5k+3,
\]
respectively. Hence the absolute value of every term of A103311 is a Fibonacci number.
